title: MB6-03051
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a stateless Palestinian whose country of habitual residence is Lebanon, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rendered on May 19, 2016, denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a stateless Palestinian whose country of habitual residence is Lebanon, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rendered on May 19, 2016, denying his claim for refugee protection.
The Appellant does not request to submit new evidence in support of his appeal and does not request a hearing before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

The Appellant requests that the RAD set aside the determination of the RPD and find the Appellant to be a "Convention refugee" according to section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) or a "person in need of protection" according to section 97.
Pursuant to s. 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD allows the appeal and refers this matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel. III. BACKGROUND a. Basis of claim
According to his Basic of Claim (BOC), the Appellant was born in Lebanon to Palestinian parents.
As an infant, he moved to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) where he was raised by his parents and completed university in business. While in the UAE, the Appellant had temporary resident status.

The Appellant and his family are officially registered as residents of the XXXX XXXX XXXX refugee camp in XXXX, Lebanon. Over the years, the Appellant returned to Lebanon to visit his grandparents who reside in the camp.

In 2006, the Appellant (then aged 16 years) travelled with his twin brother to Lebanon. The Appellant's brother was interrogated at the airport given that he shares the same name as a known criminal in Lebanon. During this encounter, airport officials humiliated and shouted at the Appellant and his brother.

In 2010, the Appellant was visiting Lebanon when he was stopped by an officer who wanted to verify his identity upon entering the XXXX XXXX XXXX refugee camp. The Appellant was interrogated by the officer who wanted to know if he was connected to a criminal named XXXX XXXX XXXX. The officer stuck the Appellant in the face and instructed him to remain in the camp until he returned to the UAE.

In 2014, the Appellant once again returned to Lebanon. While leaving the XXXX XXXX XXXX refugee camp, he was stopped by an officer who checked his identity and instructed him to return to the camp. As the incident unfolded, gunshots could be heard inside the camp. In the ensuing commotion, the Appellant injured his knee. Unable to access proper care in Lebanon, he returned to the UAE where he eventually had surgery on his knee.
In 2015, the Appellant lost his job as a XXXX XXXX in the UAE. This meant that he also lost his temporary residence permit which authorized him to re-enter the UAE.

Following the loss of his job, the Appellant did not want to relocate to Lebanon where there are many gunfights in the XXXX XXXX XXXX refugee camp to which the Lebanese authorities do not respond. In 2013, a XXXX leader named XXXX XXXX XXXX was killed by terrorists. The Appellant fears for his safety given that his family name is associated with this XXXX leader. People named "XXXX XXXX" are being targeted by terrorists and killed. The Appellant states that his relative named XXXX XXXX XXXX was killed in XXXX 2015.
Moreover, the Appellant alleges that he fears persecution based on the cumulative effect of racism and discrimination as a Palestinian in Lebanon where his basic human rights are not recognized.
The Appellant arrived in the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2015 with a student visa. On XXXX XXXX, 2015 he came to Canada and made his refugee claim on September 23, 2015.1 b. The decision of the RPD

The RPD recognized that the Appellant is a stateless Palestinian and that Lebanon is the only country of habitual residence to which he can return. The RPD rejected the Appellant's refugee claim, concluding that he is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection based on overriding concerns related to his credibility. The RPD found key aspects of the Appellant's evidence implausible and evasive and identified discrepancies which were not reasonably explained. Documentary evidence submitted to corroborate the claim could not overcome the overriding credibility concerns.

On the whole, the RPD concluded that "the Appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution in his country for being Palestinian or for any other reason, nor would there be a serious possibility of a cumulative effect of discrimination against him as a Palestinian amounting to persecution."2 c. Grounds of Appeal

The Appellant raises the following issue on appeal: - Did the RPD err in the assessment of the Appellant's credibility? - Did the RPD err by finding that the Appellant can benefit from an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Lebanon? - Did the RPD err in the analysis of the merits of the claim?
The IRPA sets out grounds for appeal and possible remedies. However, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the RPD.
paragraphs.heading_before: IV. SCOPE OF THE RAD APPEAL

paragraphs.text: In Huruglica,3 the Federal Court of Appeal held that after considering the RPD decision, the RAD is to carry out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred. The role of the RAD is to intervene when the RPD is wrong in law, in fact or in mixed fact and law, in cases which raise no issue with respect to the credibility of oral evidence. In such cases, the RAD is to apply the correctness standard of review.4 With respect to findings based on credibility of oral testimony by the RPD, the court concluded that the RAD must take a case-by-case approach to the level of deference it owes to the relative weight of oral evidence tendered at the RPD hearing.5

A recent three member panel RAD decision examined the standard of review applicable to credibility findings made by the RPD based on oral testimony. The RAD panel concluded that when the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in making a particular finding, the RAD may assess that finding using a standard of reasonableness, modified to apply to the context of the RAD.6

Guided by the principles outlined in Huruglica and the RAD panel decision, my approach to the present appeal is to analyze the record and identify any errors that may have been committed by the RPD based on the issues identified in the Memorandum of Appeal. Then, I will render a decision in light of the evidence which forms part of the record.7 When required, I will explain whether it is warranted to show deference to the RPD concerning findings of credibility based on oral evidence. When deference is warranted, I will explain how the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage with respect to the finding in question. 8

Although I may defer to findings made by the RPD with respect to the credibility of oral evidence, I will consider the RPD's determination of the refugee claim using a standard of correctness.9 V. ANALYSIS Credibility

After conducting my own analysis of the record, I find that the RPD erred in the assessment of the Appellant's credibility which is determinative of the appeal. My reasons follow. The Appellant's return to XXXX XXXX XXXX refugee camp in 2014

The RPD found it implausible that the Appellant would return to Lebanon in 2014 if he had actually been mistreated on previous trips in 2006 and 2010, as alleged. The RPD considered that the Appellant is well-educated; violence in the refugee camps in Lebanon is well documented; and the Appellant said that people who share his last name have been targeted by terrorists in the camp. As such, the RPD rejected the credibility of the Appellant's evidence that he was mistreated during past trips to Lebanon.

On appeal, it is submitted that the RPD's approach to questioning the Appellant was disparaging in nature. Moreover, the RPD unreasonably discounted the Appellant's explanation for returning to Lebanon in 2014.
Having reviewed the entirety of the record and listened to the audio recording of the hearing, I consider that the RAD is equally placed to assess the plausibility of this aspect of the evidence.10

I begin my analysis by noting that the RPD hearing is an inquisitorial process which means that it is entirely appropriate for the RPD to test the evidence by asking questions about the plausibility of the Appellant's narrative. It was incumbent on the RPD to ask questions to test the credibility of the Appellant's evidence that he was mistreated during past visits to Lebanon as this was a central issue in the case.

My review of the audio recording reveals that the RPD asked the Appellant pointed questions and challenged him when he was not satisfied with a response. However, I cannot agree that the RPD was disparaging towards the Appellant.

It is settled law that the RPD is entitled to consider plausibility, common sense and rationality when assessing a refugee claim.11 The RPD may reject evidence if it is not consistent with the probabilities affecting the case as a whole, even when that evidence is uncontradicted.

This being said, plausibility findings should be made in only the clearest of cases.12 More specifically, the Federal Court cautions that the RPD should provide "a reliable and verifiable evidentiary base against which the plausibility of an applicant's evidence might be judged, otherwise a plausibility determination may be nothing more than "unfounded speculation."13
Turning to the present case, is it plausible that the Appellant (a well-educated man) decided to return to Lebanon in 2014 if he was actually mistreated there in 2006 and 2010, as alleged?

Looking at the evidence in context, the Appellant testified that he was reluctant to return to Lebanon in 2014 but that his mother pressured him to go "one last time" to spend time with his ailing grandparents who reside in the XXXX XXXX XXXX camp. In other words, his sole purpose in returning to Lebanon in 2014 was to spend time with his relatives. When questioned about his actual activities during the 2014 trip, the Appellant maintained that his priority and focus was to spend time with his ailing grandparents.

I note that the stated purpose of his 2014 trip is consistent with previous trips to Lebanon in 2006 and 2010 which occurred at the behest of his parents and were focused on spending time with his family.

The Appellant's immediate family maintains close ties with relatives who remain in the camp which lends weight to the plausibility of his decision to return to Lebanon in 2014. Indeed, the Appellant's father continues to provide financial support to his relatives who live in the camp.

As such, I consider that the RPD erred by reaching a plausibility finding by ignoring factual details providing important context to the Appellant's decision to return to Lebanon in 2014. My analysis of the evidence leads to the conclusion that it is entirely plausible that the Appellant returned to Lebanon in 2014 for a final visit with his grandparents notwithstanding any inherent risk attached to this endeavour.

The RPD also did not believe that the Appellant returned to Lebanon in 2014 to visit his relatives based on a discrepancy in the evidence. In his BOC, the Appellant states that he returned to Lebanon in 2014 while "on vacation". At the hearing, the RPD remarked that a vacation is "to have fun, to relax, that is my general idea of a vacation."14 The RPD found that being on "vacation" is different than the detailed evidence tendered by the Appellant at the hearing to the effect that he reluctantly went to Lebanon in 2014 when pressed by his mother to visit his sick grandparents one last time in the camp.

With respect, I disagree that the word "vacation" is limited to "having fun or relaxing". The plain meaning of vacation denotes "a period spent away from home or business in travel or recreation; a scheduled period during which activity is suspended; a period of exemption from work granted to an employee; or a time of respite from something".15

In the present case, the Appellant's BOC mentions that he returned to Lebanon in 2014 while on vacation. I take this to mean that he took a trip to Lebanon while on a break from his job in the UAE in 2014. This is largely consistent with the Appellant's testimony that he went to Lebanon during his annual holiday from his job in the UAE to visit his relatives in the camp. In my view, the discrepancy identified by the RPD is not real and not rationally related to the assessment of the Appellant's credibility. Treatment of similarly situated persons in Lebanon who share the same last name as the Appellant
The Appellant testified that he will be in danger if he returns to Lebanon because people who share his last name have been targeted by terrorists in the camp.

The RPD held that the Appellant's evidence is not credible given that "similarly situated persons" such as the Appellant's twin brother, father and grandfather have not mentioned experiencing any problems with the authorities in Lebanon nor have they mentioned having problems as Palestinians in Lebanon as a result of being associated with the "XXXX XXXX" name.
On appeal, it is argued that the RPD misapprehended the facts and erred in the analysis of similarly situated persons.

I have carefully reviewed the Appellant's testimony and documentary evidence. I consider that the RAD is equally placed to assess the Appellant's evidence concerning "similarly situated persons" such that the RPD does not benefit from any meaningful advantage in assessing this aspect of the Appellant's credibility.

I note at the outset that the RPD was correct to proceed with an analysis of "similarly situated persons" in the present case. After all, the RPD is entitled to consider whether a claimant has established persecution under s. 96 of the IRPA through the treatment of similarly situated individuals to that of the refugee claimant.16

This being said, I have identified two key errors in the assessment conducted by the RPD which renders the adverse credibility finding unsustainable: first, the foundation of this finding is based on factual errors. Secondly, the RPD failed to consider critical evidence regarding similarly situated persons.

The factual errors are summarized as follows: - The RPD determined that the Appellant's assertion that he is at risk in Lebanon strains credibility because his twin brother, being a similarly situated person, visited Lebanon in 2015 and did not report any danger to the Appellant even though he spent 23 days visiting his grandparents.17 On the face of it, 23 days seems like a reasonable period of time to assess how the brother was treated. However, the Appellant did not say that his brother visited Lebanon for 23 days. He clearly testified that his brother spent "maybe 2 or 3 days only" visiting his grandparents when he returned to Lebanon in 2015. - The RPD found that the Appellant's father and grandfather did not experience any problems in Lebanon as a result of the fact that they share the same name as a known terrorist. However, this finding is not an accurate reflection of the evidence. Rather, the Appellant testified that his grandfather is an old man who is ill. Both his father and grandfather suffered a lot in the past as a result of living though the war. As such, he "never discusses with his grandfather if he suffered with anything"18 and he never asked his father and grandfather if they experienced problems in Lebanon.

The RPD reached the conclusion that "similarly situated persons" such as the Appellant's twin brother, father and grandfather did not experience problems with the authorities in Lebanon nor did they experience problems as Palestinians in Lebanon based in part, on a misapprehension of the evidence.

This finding is not trivial since it led the RPD to disbelieve the credibility of the Appellant's assertion that he is in danger if he returns to Lebanon as a result of the fact that people with his name are targeted by terrorists. Most significantly, this also led the RPD to reject news articles produced by the Appellant about a terrorist named XXXX XXXX XXXX, a XXXX official named XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX killed in 2012 and a person named XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX killed by two Islamic militants in 2008. The documentary evidence was rejected by the RPD based on the erroneous finding that the Appellant "testified that he was not aware of any of his other family members with the same name having problems in Lebanon." It is plain to see that the factual errors made by the RPD had a far reaching impact on the overall decision to reject the credibility of this aspect of the claim.

Secondly, I note that the RPD limited the inquiry of "similarly situated persons" to the Appellant's brother, father and grandfather. This manner of proceeding means that the RPD failed to consider other relevant information found in the Appellant's BOC stating that the Appellant's relative XXXX XXXX XXXX was killed by terrorists in the camp on XXXX XXXX, 2015. To be clear, I note the following excerpt in the Appellant's BOC: "XXXX XXXX XXXX is a refugee camp for Palestinian refugees. People there are trying to survive every day. It is not safe at all, there are many gun fights happening that cannot be stopped by the Lebanese authorities because they are refusing to go inside the camp. So it is dangerous to live there. In 2013, the XXXX XXXX XXXX whose name was XXXX XXXX XXXX got killed by the terrorist group called Al Salafy'in. Since that day, people with that name are getting targeted and killed. The fights between those two groups never stopped which leads innocent people getting killed just because of the family name. One of my relative got killed on the XXXX of XXXX 2015, his name was XXXX XXXX XXXX."

This passage from the Appellant's BOC is highly relevant to the analysis of "similarly situated persons" yet the RPD has not considered this information in the analysis. Moreover, my review of the audio recording reveals that this issue was never canvassed with the Appellant at the hearing.

In sum, the RPD did not believe that the Appellant faces any danger if he returns to Lebanon on the basis that people associated with his name are targeted by terrorists in the camp. This finding is unsustainable given that the RPD failed to consider all the Appellant's available evidence concerning "similarly situated individuals." Ability of the Appellant to live outside the XXXX XXXX XXXX camp based on the affluence of his father

While acknowledging the difficult circumstances that prevail in the XXXX XXXX XXXX camp, the RPD asked the Appellant if he could rent an apartment outside the camp upon his return to Lebanon. The Appellant explained that it would be difficult for him to get an apartment outside the camp because he does not have the financial means to do so and he would be unable to find a job in Lebanon where he faces discrimination as a Palestinian. When confronted with the fact that his father who works in the UAE, guaranteed $200,000 as security so that the Appellant could obtain a student visa to the United States, the Appellant conceded that his father would undoubtedly come to his aid if he found himself in a dire situation requiring financial assistance upon his return to Lebanon.

The RPD found the Appellant's evidence to be evasive with respect to his family's wealth and his father's ability to support him. The RPD concluded that this aspect of the "Appellant's evidence is unsatisfactory and undermines his credibility regarding his financial means to live outside the refugee camp as an internal flight alternative (IFA)."19

I will state at the outset that the RPD is entitled to reach a negative credibility finding when the claimant's evidence is couched in vague terms. After all, this type of evidence may be a strong indicator that a witness is attempting to be evasive.20

Here, the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage in assessing the Appellant's oral testimony for signs of vagueness. The RPD had the advantage of posing the questions, hearing the testimony and observing the witness.21 As such deference is owed to the RPD which means that I will assess this finding on a reasonableness standard.22

I have reviewed the record and audio recording of the RPD which reveals that the Appellant's testimony was forthright about the fact that his father guaranteed an amount of $200,000 as security so that he could obtain his student visa to the USA. Likewise, he was forthright about the fact that his father would help him out if he was required to return to Lebanon and needed financial assistance. There is no evidence that he tried to conceal or distort this information which is also mentioned in his visa application. In my view, the Appellant's evidence concerning his father's financial situation cannot reasonably be said to be evasive to the extent that it undermined his credibility.

Moreover, I must agree with Appellant's counsel who submits that the RPD engaged in speculation when reaching the conclusion that the Appellant should be able to count on his father's generosity to support him for an indefinite period of time in Lebanon. This finding is flawed because it is a guess. Simply put, there is no evidence that the Appellant's father is actually willing or able to care for him. To the contrary, the Appellant's evidence is that his father is already taxed with caring for several other family members. Moreover, the RPD's speculative expectation that the Appellant's father should support him indefinitely ignores the fact that the Appellant is a 26 year old man who is presenting his refugee claim on an individual basis. Documentary evidence

The RPD accepted some of the documentary evidence provided by the Appellant while rejecting other documents as not probative. For instance, the RPD gave probative weight to documents produced after the hearing recognizing that the Appellant is officially registered as residing at the XXXX XXXX XXXX refugee camp and that Lebanon is the only country of habitual residence where the Appellant, as a stateless Palestinian, can return.23

On the other hand, no probative weight was given to documentary information submitted by the Appellant about the treatment of Palestinians in Lebanon.24 The RPD noted that these documents are similar in nature to information found in the NDP for Lebanon which describes "similar treatment of Palestinians, including restrictions on property ownership, restrictions from certain kinds of professions and restricted access to public health and education services in Lebanon."25 The RPD rationale for setting aside this documentary information is described as follows: "The claimant's probative evidence regarding his personal circumstances as a Palestinian in Lebanon, considered with his lack of credibility regarding past mistreatment in Lebanon and considered with the objective evidence regarding the treatment of Palestinians generally in Lebanon, does not show that the claimant would face a serious possibility of persecution or the cumulative effect of discrimination amounting to persecution." (emphasis added)
On appeal it is submitted that the conclusion reached by the RPD is arbitrary and not founded on the evidence. I agree with this submission.

The RPD states that it has considered the objective evidence regarding the treatment of Palestinians generally in Lebanon and concludes that this objective evidence does not show that the claimant would face a serious possibility of persecution or the cumulative effect of discrimination amounting to persecution. However, the RPD failed to articulate any reasons to explain why the documentary evidence concerning the conditions of Palestinians living in Lebanon does not amount to persecution. The lack of reasons is striking, particularly in light of the fact that the RPD acknowledged that documentary evidence demonstrates "restrictions" on Palestinians living in Lebanon.
In sum, the RPD erred because this finding is not supported by any analysis or explanation.
In conclusion, I have independently analyzed the record,26 listened to the audio recording, considered the Appellants' arguments and reviewed the RPD decision.

In the present case, the RPD identified credibility as the central issue. While it was open for the RPD to make adverse credibility findings based on testimony that was evasive, implausible and contradictory, my review of the evidence has led me to identify several errors in the RPD's findings which are unsustainable and determinative of the appeal.

This being said, I am unable to confirm or substitute the RPD decision without hearing the Appellant's oral testimony and weighing evidence presented by the Appellant with respect to his credibility.27
Therefore, pursuant to ss. 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, I refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel.

The appeal is allowed.
